clue.text: They're no longer public information

parts.note: things kept back from general knowledge are confidential matters, but the phrase reads like a news item about archives closing

explanation.surface: A remark about documents that have been withdrawn from public view.
explanation.definitionFit: Confidential matters are by nature information withheld from general knowledge.

clue.text: Dog in a pound makes a home in his new territory

definitions.text: makes a home in his new territory
definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the person who does this, a colonist

indicators.note: the pound sits inside the dog's name, so in signals one piece placed within another

parts.note: a setter is a breed of gun dog
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A stray dog taken to the pound settles into its new surroundings.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonist is someone who moves to a new land and establishes a home there.

clue.text: Get them from milk round, usually

definitions.text: Get them from milk round, usually

parts.words: Get them from milk round, usually
parts.note: dairy products made from milk are usually round wheels, while the surface suggests a milkman's delivery round

explanation.surface: Advice that certain goods are usually bought from the milkman on his round.
explanation.definitionFit: Dairy products such as Cheddar and Brie are made from milk and commonly formed in round wheels.

clue.text: Brief report saying all about the enemy!

definitions.text: Brief report saying all about the enemy!

parts.words: Brief report saying all about the enemy!
parts.note: a terse battlefield dispatch saying the enemy has been surrounded on all sides

explanation.surface: A short military dispatch giving the full story of the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All about' looks like 'everything concerning', but it means surrounding on every side, which is what a short war bulletin would announce.
explanation.definitionFit: Surrounded on all sides, ringed in, as an army does to its foe.

clue.text: Female has two articles to put in the scabbard

parts.note: she is the female pronoun
a is the indefinite article
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A woman has a pair of items to slide into a sword's scabbard.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a blade back into its case or scabbard is the verb used for that action.

clue.text: Angler's helper: red-head gone after it. Obviously not a sinker!

definitions.note: past-tense verb sense: something that drifted on the surface clearly did not sink

parts.note: a float is the bobbing marker an angler uses on the line

indicators.note: the first letter of the word red is dropped, its head removed

explanation.surface: A fishing float with a red top has gone, and clearly it did not sink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After it' places ED, red without its head, after the float. A sinker is the weight on a fishing line, the opposite of a float.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that stayed on the surface of water clearly did not go down like a weight.

clue.text: Gets bad infection

parts.note: a wound that turns septic and gets worse, read as though someone catches a nasty infection

explanation.surface: Someone comes down with a nasty infection.
explanation.definitionFit: A wound that suppurates and worsens through infection is said to do this.

clue.text: Upset Shropshire jewellers EC 4 P with them

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Upset Shropshire jewellers EC 4 P with them' is garbled: SALOP upset gives the answer, but 'EC 4 P' is an OCR misread of lost words and the definition cannot be identified.
annotationWithheld.clue: Upset Shropshire jewellers EC 4 P with them

clue.text: Went down to the bo tom!

definitions.text: Went down to the bo tom!

parts.words: Went down to the bo tom!
parts.note: narrowed gradually to a point, read as though someone descended to the very bottom

explanation.surface: Someone descended all the way to the lowest point.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held reads 'bo tom' for 'bottom', a gap in the print; 'went down' means diminished in width toward the base.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that narrows steadily toward one end, like a candle or a trouser leg, is said to have done this.

clue.text: Ridicules the German before Roman times

parts.note: der is the German masculine definite article
the Ides were fixed days in the Roman calendar, mid-month

explanation.surface: Someone mocks the German for coming before the era of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean to mock or make fun of someone scornfully.

clue.text: Sweet& tart

parts.note: a dark sugary syrup, which with the word tart makes a classic British pudding

explanation.surface: A dessert that is at once sweet and sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tart' looks like sour, the opposite of sweet, but here it is a pastry: a treacle tart is a traditional British dessert of golden syrup baked in pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: This thick dark syrup is a sweet, and it fills the traditional tart named after it.

clue.text: Like this, it's easier to cut for cheat at cards

definitions.text: Like this, it's easier to cut
definitions.meaning: comparative of keen-edged: a blade with a finer edge slices more easily
a card swindler, an old word for a gambling cheat

explanation.definitionFit: A keener blade cuts better, and a card swindler is an old noun meaning a cheating gambler.

clue.text: Best person to make him so

definitions.text: Best person to make him so

parts.words: Best person to make him so
parts.note: to best someone is to beat them, which makes the defeated party the one who did not win

explanation.surface: Someone who is the ideal choice for a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like an adjective meaning finest, but it is a verb: beat a person and you make them the defeated one.
explanation.definitionFit: One who has been beaten in a contest is the defeated party.

clue.text: Certain about a footstep being highly valued

indicators.note: the footstep goes around the word for certain, so about signals one piece enclosing another

parts.note: a tread is a single step or the sound of one
sure means certain

explanation.surface: Being sure of a footstep makes it precious.
explanation.definitionFit: Something held dear and cherished is greatly prized.

clue.text: Decide to crack the problem

definitions.meaning: to determine firmly on a course of action
to settle or clear up a difficulty, find its solution

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to make up one's mind and to settle a difficulty.

clue.text: Goes for a walk to stretch one's legs!

definitions.text: Goes for a walk to stretch one's legs!

parts.words: Goes for a walk to stretch one's legs!
parts.note: taking long steps literally stretches the legs, while the idiom means a gentle walk

explanation.surface: Someone takes a stroll to get some exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch one's legs' is the idiom for a short walk, but taken literally it describes taking long paces.
explanation.definitionFit: Long paces made by walking with a wide gait are long steps.

clue.text: They must be able to fight back an army

definitions.text: They must be able to fight back an army

parts.words: They must be able to fight back an army
parts.note: troops posted at the back of an army who fight there, read as though they repel an enemy army

explanation.surface: Defenders who must be strong enough to repel a whole army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fight back' suggests resisting an attack; here it means fighting at the back of an army.
explanation.definitionFit: The troops protecting the back of a marching army are its rear defensive force.

clue.text: Puts No I into No 2 for No 3

definitions.text: Puts No I into No 2 for No 3

parts.words: Puts No I into No 2 for No 3
parts.note: arithmetic phrasing: how many times one number goes into another to give a third

explanation.surface: Instructions that read like a cross-reference to other numbered clues.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers look like crossword cross-references, but the sentence is arithmetic: putting one number into another is splitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: In arithmetic, finding how often one number goes into another is the operation of splitting.

clue.text: Wages mean little to such workers

definitions.text: Wages mean little to such workers

parts.words: Wages mean little to such workers
parts.note: menial labourers paid a mean wage, i.e. a meagre one, read as though money does not matter to them

explanation.surface: Workers who are indifferent to how much they are paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean little' looks like 'matter little', but 'mean' is the adjective for stingy: their wages are mean and little.
explanation.definitionFit: Labourers doing dull, hard, poorly paid work are menial toilers.

clue.text: Brave type of Latvian

indicators.note: the letters of the nationality are rearranged into another type, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: A courageous kind of person from Latvia.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean courageous and bold in the face of danger.

clue.text: Wound threads used on it

parts.note: surgical stitches used on a wound, read as though threads that have been wound on a reel

explanation.surface: Thread that has been wound and then used on something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' reads as the past tense of wind, as for thread on a spool, but it is the injury that stitches close.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgical stitches are threads used to close an injury.

clue.text: One who applauds a bell-ringer

definitions.meaning: someone striking hands together in appreciation
the tongue inside a bell that strikes it to make it ring

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a person who claps and the swinging tongue that sounds a bell.

clue.text: Will add one to it, or 10005001100150!

parts.note: the run of digits splits as 100, 0, 500, 1, 100, 1, 50, and each value is a Roman numeral or the letter O

explanation.surface: A will can take an addition, or a long string of figures.
explanation.walkthrough: In Roman numerals C is 100, D 500, I 1 and L 50, while the 0 stands for the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A supplement added to a will, amending or extending it, is this legal document.

clue.text: Make one in a rage lose it

definitions.text: Make one in a rage lose it

parts.words: Make one in a rage lose it
parts.note: to soothe an angry person so the anger goes, while 'lose it' usually means to become furious

explanation.surface: Provoking an already furious person into losing their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose it' is the idiom for losing one's temper, but here 'it' is the rage itself, which is soothed away.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease or pacify someone angry is to calm them down.

clue.text: Makes meals of rotten pears on the way back

indicators.note: rotten fruit falls apart, so the letters of pears are broken up and rearranged
the abbreviation for the way is read backwards, as if travelling back

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Someone makes dinners out of decaying pears while on the journey home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten' makes REPAS from PEARS, and 'back' turns ST into TS.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal word for meals or food eaten at one sitting.

clue.text: Company not registered as having infinite resources?

definitions.text: Company not registered as having infinite resources?

parts.words: Company not registered as having infinite resources?
parts.note: a firm not registered as limited liability, read as though its resources had no limit

explanation.surface: A business that is not officially registered appears to have endless wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: In British company law a firm registered without limited liability is an 'unlimited company', its members liable for all its debts.
explanation.definitionFit: Boundless, without any limit, and also the term for a company whose members have no liability cap.

clue.text: Sounds the most important

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Sounds the most important' gives MAIN aloud, but no word defines the US state; a defining word appears lost in the OCR.

clue.text: Apprehend and hold!

definitions.meaning: to understand or take in mentally

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to comprehend an idea and to seize something tightly.

clue.text: Window-shoppers generally stop at his establishment

definitions.text: Window-shoppers generally stop at his establishment

parts.words: Window-shoppers generally stop at his establishment
parts.note: people shopping for windows, i.e. panes of glass, go to this tradesman, while window-shopping means browsing

explanation.surface: Browsers looking in shop windows tend to pause outside a particular shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Window-shoppers usually means browsers who only look; here they are people actually buying windows.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who fits panes of glass into windows sells to people wanting windows.

clue.text: Women are less likely to have them on broken-down cars without tax

definitions.text: Women are less likely to have them on

indicators.note: the jumbled cars sit outside the tax, without being the old sense of outside
broken-down cars are wrecked, so the letters of cars are rearranged

parts.note: VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax

explanation.surface: Women are less likely to drive wrecked, untaxed cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have them on' means wear: neckties are mostly men's wear. 'Without' here is the old sense of outside, so the scrambled letters wrap round the tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Neckwear of this kind, a tie or scarf, is traditionally worn by men rather than women.

clue.text: Theycan'tstand being artists'models

parts.note: people who pose seated for a painter cannot stand up, read as though they hate modelling

explanation.surface: People who hate being artists' models.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't stand' looks like 'hate', but it is literal: those posing must remain seated. The held text runs words together from the print.
explanation.definitionFit: Models who pose seated for a portrait are those in the chair.

clue.text: Bound to keep the accounts

parts.note: bound books used for keeping accounts, read as though someone is obliged to do the bookkeeping

explanation.surface: Someone is obliged to look after the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'obliged', but it describes bound volumes in which accounts are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Account books in which financial transactions are recorded are bound books.
